**Answer: The statement is TRUE.**

## Proof

Let $G$ be a finite group and $g_1, g_2 \in G$. Since every finite-dimensional complex representation decomposes (by complete reducibility, Maschke's theorem) as a direct sum of irreducible representations, the hypothesis

$$\chi_\rho(g_1)=\chi_\rho(g_2)\quad\text{for every representation }\rho$$

is equivalent to

$$\chi_i(g_1)=\chi_i(g_2)\quad\text{for every irreducible character }\chi_1,\dots,\chi_h,$$

where $h$ is the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.

We use the **column orthogonality relation** for the character table. For any $g,h\in G$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^{h}\chi_i(g)\,\overline{\chi_i(h)}=\begin{cases}|C_G(g)|,& g\sim h,\\[2pt]0,& g\not\sim h,\end{cases}$$

where $C_G(g)=\{x\in G:xg=gx\}$ is the centralizer of $g$ (so $|C_G(g)|=|G|/|\mathrm{Cl}(g)|\ge 1$), and $\sim$ denotes conjugacy.

Apply this twice. First, with $g=h=g_1$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{h}\chi_i(g_1)\,\overline{\chi_i(g_1)}=|C_G(g_1)|.\tag{1}$$

Second, with $g=g_1,\;h=g_2$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{h}\chi_i(g_1)\,\overline{\chi_i(g_2)}=\begin{cases}|C_G(g_1)|,& g_1\sim g_2,\\[2pt]0,& g_1\not\sim g_2.\end{cases}\tag{2}$$

By the hypothesis $\chi_i(g_1)=\chi_i(g_2)$ for all $i$, we have $\overline{\chi_i(g_2)}=\overline{\chi_i(g_1)}$, so the left-hand side of (2) equals the left-hand side of (1), namely $|C_G(g_1)|$.

Therefore the right-hand side of (2) must equal $|C_G(g_1)|$. The second branch of (2) would force $|C_G(g_1)|=0$, which is impossible since the identity (and at least $g_1$ itself) centralizes $g_1$, giving $|C_G(g_1)|\ge 1$. Hence the first branch must hold:

$$g_1\sim g_2.$$

Thus $g_1$ and $g_2$ belong to the same conjugacy class. $\blacksquare$
